svg.aria-label: Azure default outbound access and its retirement: what the behaviour is, the API-version mechanism rather than a cutoff date, the four explicit replacements, and what breaks in a private subnet
svg.title: Azure default outbound access and its retirement: a default value changing for new virtual networks on new API versions, not a dated shutdown
svg.text: Not a shutdown. A default flip — which is why two pipelines can now disagree.
THE BEHAVIOUR
A VM deployed with no explicit outbound method is automatically given an outbound public IP.
That address is owned by Microsoft and can change without notice.
It is an implicit platform behaviour, not a resource you configure — so there is nothing to inspect.
THE ACTUAL MECHANISM — SCOPED THREE WAYS
New VNet, API version after 31 March 2026
PRIVATE — explicit outbound required
New VNet via the Azure portal
PRIVATE ALREADY
New VNet, earlier API version
default outbound still granted
New VM in an existing VNet
default outbound still granted
Any subnet explicitly set nonprivate
default outbound still granted
Earlier ARM template versions, and tools like Terraform pinned to them, leave the property null —
which implicitly allows outbound. Both paths deploy successfully and neither reports a difference.
THE FOUR EXPLICIT REPLACEMENTS
· NAT gateway on the subnet — the recommended method for most scenarios
· Standard load balancer with outbound rules, VM in the backend pool
· A Standard public IP on the machine’s network interface
· A firewall or network virtual appliance, pointed at by a user-defined route
WHAT MAKING A SUBNET PRIVATE COSTS
· User-defined routes with next hop type Internet break. That is the firewall-with-exceptions
pattern: everything to the NVA, except named service tags bypassed via Internet.
Service endpoints are unaffected — different next hop type, and not overridable.
· Windows Activation and Windows Updates stop working without explicit egress.
· Existing VMs must be stopped and deallocated for the change to take effect — in both directions,
so the rollback is as disruptive as the change.
· Same-region Azure Storage is still reachable. Private is not isolated; use an NSG for egress.
· Not applicable to delegated or managed subnets — the service owns their egress.
· A load balancer backend pool configured by IP still uses default outbound: a known issue.
THE SYMPTOMS THAT NEVER MADE SENSE
Default outbound access IPs support neither fragmented packets nor ICMP pings.
Multiple NICs give inconsistent outbound IPs; scale set instances give changing, non-contiguous ones.
A VM that cannot ping and loses large UDP payloads is not broken and its NSG is not wrong.
FINDING OUT WHERE YOU STAND
The NIC parameter defaultOutboundConnectivityEnabled drives a portal banner. Azure Advisor carries
two separate Operational Excellence recommendations — one for VMs, one for scale sets.
